summary: Defines SNMP management objects for Ethernet-like interfaces. It replaced RFC 2358 and was replaced by RFC 3635.

plainLanguage.summary: Readouts for the standard wired network port, such as how many errors or collisions happened.

questions: how do you monitor ethernet interfaces with snmp
subtitle: SNMP objects for monitoring Ethernet interfaces at all speeds.

tldr.problem: Ethernet networks exist at multiple speeds (10 Mb/s, 100 Mb/s, 1000 Mb/s, and full-duplex variants), and network operators need a standard way to monitor errors, collisions, and performance across all Ethernet interfaces regardless of speed or vendor.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SNMP MIB objects that represent Ethernet interface statistics, tests, and properties. All Ethernet speeds use the same MIB and the same ifType, with speed determined through ifSpeed and ifHighSpeed objects.
tldr.outcome: Network management tools can now uniformly monitor all Ethernet interfaces. The RFC superseded RFC 2358 and was replaced by RFC 3635 to cover newer Ethernet technologies.

today: RFC 2665 is a Proposed Standard that defines Ethernet interface management objects. It was superseded by RFC 3635, which extends the specification to cover newer Ethernet technologies and capabilities.

sections.title: Ethernet Interface Management
sections.content:
This RFC defines the Management Information Base (MIB) module for Ethernet-like interfaces. Ethernet is defined by the IEEE 802.3 Working Group and continues to evolve with new speeds and capabilities. The RFC covers ethernetCsmacd (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection), the dominant Ethernet mechanism at all speeds.

The MIB applies to interfaces at any speed: 10 Mb/s, 100 Mb/s, 1000 Mb/s, and full-duplex variants. The RFC recommends that all Ethernet interfaces use the same ifType value (ethernetCsmacd) regardless of speed, with the actual speed available through ifSpeed and ifHighSpeed objects.
sections.plainLanguage: Whether a network wire is slow, fast, or super-fast, it is still Ethernet, and the monitoring questions are the same. The program just checks which speed it is separately.

sections.title: Statistics and Error Counting
sections.content:
The Statistics Table (dot3StatsTable) counts Ethernet MAC layer errors: frames transmitted and received, octets transmitted and received, deferred transmissions, collisions, alignment errors, frame check sequence errors, frame too long errors, and symbol errors. A separate Receive Address Table (ifRcvAddressTable) lists all MAC addresses (unicast, multicast, and broadcast) for which the interface will accept frames.

The MIB defines standard frame sizes and MAC addresses. The physical address is stored in binary in canonical bit order, where the Group Bit is the low-order bit of the first octet. The default MTU (Maximum Transmission Unit) for Ethernet is 1500 octets as seen by higher-layer protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The system counts how many messages went in and out, how many errors happened, and what addresses the wire listens to. This is like counting traffic and mistakes.

sections.title: Testing and Diagnostics
sections.content:
The RFC defines two optional diagnostic tests for Ethernet interfaces: TDR (Time Domain Reflectometry), which measures cable length and detects breaks, and Loopback, which tests the interface by looping transmitted frames back to the receiver. Implementation of these tests is optional, as many interface chips do not support them.

The ifTestTable provides a standard method to invoke tests, though the RFC notes that this table is now deprecated. Results of TDR tests are not standardized and must be provided through vendor-specific MIB extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the port can test itself by sending a message and listening for it to come back, like shouting in a tunnel to hear your echo.

sections.title: MAU Types and Chip Sets
sections.content:
The RFC relates to the IEEE 802.3 MAU (Medium Attachment Unit) MIB, which describes the media attachment hardware. Ethernet interfaces may report their chip set via dot3StatsEtherChipSet, though this is optional. The RFC clarifies that Ethernet-like interfaces do not inherently support layering, virtual circuits, or sublayers, though vendors could add 802.2 LLC or transceiver sublayers as extensions.

For bridges (devices that forward frames between Ethernet ports), the RFC clarifies that the ifRcvAddressTable does not include unicast addresses accepted for possible forwarding, as this table is not intended to provide bridge address filtering.
sections.plainLanguage: Different Ethernet cards have different internals. The MIB lets you ask which chip is inside, if the card chooses to tell you.

sections.title: IEEE 802.3 and Interface Mapping
sections.content:
The definitions are based on IEEE Standard 802.3, 1998 Edition, Section 30, which includes management specifications for 10, 100, and 1000 Mb/s Ethernet. Implementors should note that IEEE 802.3 explicitly describes when, where, and how various MAC attributes are measured, and the effects of MAC actions invoked by manipulating MIB objects.

The RFC avoids redundantly defining objects already covered in MIB-2 or the Interfaces MIB, such as octet counts, frame counts, promiscuous status, and multicast information. A one-to-one relationship exists between Ethernet-like interfaces and Interfaces MIB entries, so an ifIndex value directly identifies corresponding MIB objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The document follows the rules in the IEEE standard for how Ethernet works. Different parts of the MIB cover different aspects, and they fit together like puzzle pieces.
